prime.problem: "Which model?" isn't enough to say how fast a response will be. The same gpt-oss-120b weights run 36× faster on one host than another, and the reasons (chip, precision, speculative decoding, how many users share a chip) are mostly unpublished.
prime.fits: The synthesis for the mechanism part. Memory bandwidth, hardware, quantization and speculative decoding each explained one factor; this card multiplies them into one host's speed and shows where to look the numbers up.
expect: speed ≈ bandwidth ÷ bytes per token × tokens per pass ÷ users sharing
per-host precision, output cap and price
prime.goal: Explain why two hosts of the same model differ in speed, and pick a host with the right numbers in hand.

attend: Which of the four factors in the host formula can you see on a provider page, and which can you only infer from measured speed?
Why does TTFT barely differ across the nine hosts while output speed varies 36×?
CoreWeave and Baseten both list fp4. Why doesn't that make them equally fast?
Why is there no fast tier to pick for Claude Sonnet 5?
When does a host's output cap matter for a reasoning model?

must: Each token reads the active weights once → one user's speed ≈ chip bandwidth ÷ bytes per token × tokens per pass ÷ users sharing the chip → the host chooses every factor except the model

The GPU ceiling for gpt-oss-120b is about 1,240 t/s but GPU hosts deliver 48–334 → most of the gap is sharing and overhead → the one factor hosts never publish (batch size) explains most of the spread
Output speed is an outside median measured a few times a day → it moves with load and says nothing about quality → check precision, price and uptime before picking the fastest
elevated: Thinking counts toward the output cap → a 16,384-token cap can cut off a long high-effort answer → check the cap before choosing a host for reasoning models
reference: the nine hosts' speeds, TTFTs and prices

compress.prompt: Close the card and write the four-factor host formula from memory. Next to each factor, name the course card that explains it and one host fact that shows it. Then say in one sentence why the same model can be 36× apart.
checklist: bandwidth (hardware / memory-bandwidth): SRAM hosts at 80+ TB/s and 21 PB/s
bytes per token (quantization, MoE): fp4 vs bf16 in the precision column
tokens per pass (speculative decoding): typically 2–3×, never published
users sharing (batching): inferred from measured speed far below the ceiling
TTFT spread is small (0.28–1.35 s), so the gap is per-token speed

retrieve.q: Explain why output speed on Artificial Analysis is not the same thing as a host's throughput, and which one you should compare hosts on.
answer: output speed: one ordinary request's tokens/s after the first token, measured from outside
throughput: the server's total across all users
compare on per-request speed; throughput can rise while your speed falls

retrieve.q: Walk through the estimate of gpt-oss-120b's single-user ceiling on one H100, and say what each measured number implies.
answer: GPU hosts at 48–334 t/s lose most of it to sharing and overhead; Cerebras at 1,745 isn't bandwidth-limited at all

retrieve.q: DeepInfra Turbo costs about 3.5× standard DeepInfra and is about 7× faster. For a nightly batch job and for a live coding assistant, which do you pick?
answer: batch job: nobody waits, so the cheaper standard tier
coding assistant: a person waits on long answers, so Turbo
check that the precision (both bf16 here) and output cap suit the task

compare.q: The hardware card explained the 36× spread mostly by chips. What does this card add that hardware alone can't explain, and which two hosts show it?
answer: same chip class can still differ widely because of sharing, precision and speculative decoding
DeepInfra Turbo (334 t/s) vs DeepInfra standard (48 t/s): same company, very different speeds
CoreWeave and Baseten both fp4 but 65 vs 273 t/s

compare.q: Artificial Analysis sends a few requests a day; a serving benchmark sweeps load. What can a load sweep reveal about a host that a daily median hides?
answer: how per-request speed and TTFT degrade as concurrency rises
the tail (p95/p99), not just the median
the median is one point on a curve that moves with the host's load

predict.q: A host moves gpt-oss-120b from bf16 to fp4 on the same GPUs and the same batch size. Predict the change in the bandwidth ceiling and in delivered speed, and one reason delivered speed won't rise by the full factor.
predict.answer: Bytes per token roughly quarter (16 → 4 bits), so the ceiling rises up to ~4×. Delivered speed rises less: dequantization costs compute, attention and KV-cache reads don't shrink with weight precision, and sharing overhead stays. Quality may also drop, which the speed number won't show.

apply.task: Pick an open model you'd use. On Artificial Analysis's provider page and OpenRouter's provider tab, collect for three hosts: output speed, TTFT, precision, output cap and price. Compute the end-to-end time for your typical answer length on each, and choose a host for (a) a chat app and (b) an overnight batch job.
apply.done: You have a 3-row table, an end-to-end time per host from TTFT + tokens ÷ speed, and two choices that each cite at least one non-speed factor (precision, price, cap).
apply.hint: For gpt-oss-120b: Cerebras 1,745 t/s at 0.50 s; Baseten 273 t/s at 0.28 s (fp4); DeepInfra 48 t/s at 0.65 s (bf16).
